0.title: Free to See, Called to Purity
0.essay:
You are walking down the street, or standing in a queue, or sitting in church. Someone walks past, and you notice that she is beautiful, or that he is handsome. That is all. No fantasy, no plan, no wish. And yet a heaviness settles on you. You feel dirty, disloyal, guilty. The feeling follows you for hours. Tomorrow it will happen again. If you know that experience, this study is for you.

A question worth asking

This study began with a question from a married Christian man. He wrote that whenever he sees a woman he finds attractive, even without any sexual thought at all, he already feels bad, and the feeling stays with him for a long time. He struggles with it nearly every day. Many believers, men and women, married and single, would say the same. Some have never told anyone.

The question is a good one, because it comes from a good place. It comes from a heart that wants to be faithful to God and to a spouse, and takes Jesus’ words seriously. But a tender conscience can be misinformed. It can sound the alarm where God has not, and keep sounding it long after the danger has passed.

Two things at once

This study will try to hold together two things that are often pulled apart. The first is the real call to purity. Jesus’ words about lustful looking are not softened here, and lust is a real sin with real power. The second is real freedom. Noticing beauty is not lust. Being tempted is not sinning. A believer in Christ does not live under a cloud, because Christ has carried the storm. We will look at what God says about beauty, what Jesus actually forbids, why the conscience sometimes misfires, what the gospel does for a troubled conscience, and what to do in the moment and afterwards.

The study Biblical Sexuality sets out God’s design for sex and marriage, and Fighting Sin & Temptation covers temptation more broadly. This study builds on them without repeating them.

The chapters

The Cloud After the Glance; Beauty Is God’s Idea; What Jesus Actually Forbids; False Guilt and True Guilt; A Clean Conscience in Christ; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

When did you last feel guilty after simply noticing someone? Did you ask whether you had actually done anything wrong, or did the feeling decide for you?

1.title: The Cloud After the Glance
1.essay:
It takes less than a second. A face in the crowd, a colleague at the next desk, a stranger at the petrol station. You register that she is lovely, and you look away. Then, before you have taken another step, the verdict arrives: you should not have noticed that. What kind of husband are you? What kind of Christian?

What happens inside

For many people the glance itself is over almost at once. What lasts is what follows. A low cloud of guilt settles over the morning. You replay the moment and examine it. Did I look too long? Did I feel something? Was there desire in it? You cannot quite answer, so you assume the worst. You feel you ought to confess something, but you are not sure what. You may feel you have betrayed your wife or husband, though you have done nothing to them at all.

The cloud can last all day. It makes prayer feel awkward, because you feel you must first deal with your guilt, and you never quite manage it. It can make you tense around the people you have noticed, avoiding eye contact, becoming stiff and unfriendly, as if a pleasant face were a trap. And because the world is full of faces, the struggle returns tomorrow, and the next day.

Not only men

This is often spoken of as a man’s struggle, and many men know it well. But women know it too. A woman notices a handsome man at work or at church and feels a stab of shame, as though noticing were already unfaithfulness. Sometimes women feel it all the more because they have heard the issue discussed only as a male problem, and assume something must be especially wrong with them. Everything in this study applies to both.

Three things that feel alike

Part of the trouble is that three different things can feel the same to a troubled conscience. The first is noticing: seeing that a person is attractive, as you might notice that a sunset is beautiful or a voice is lovely. The second is temptation: a pull, perhaps a flicker of interest, an invitation to look again or let the mind wander. The third is lust: choosing to look in order to desire, letting the mind take possession of a person in imagination, welcoming the fantasy and dwelling in it.

Scripture treats these three very differently. The first is part of being a creature in a beautiful world. The second is the common experience of every believer, including the sinless Son of God. Only the third is the sin Jesus names. A great deal of needless suffering comes from treating the first two as if they were the third.

Why it hurts so much

Often this struggle grows in good soil. You love your spouse. You fear God. You have read Jesus’ words about the eye and the heart and you do not want to play games with them. You may have seen marriages destroyed by unfaithfulness, or you may carry memories of past sin, perhaps with pornography, which make you watchful, even jumpy. Some of us were taught as teenagers that every attraction is dangerous, and never unlearned it.

For others, the cloud has a different source: an anxious temperament, a perfectionist streak, or a mind that seizes on a thought and cannot let it go. Later chapters will say more about this. For now it is enough to say that the strength of a feeling of guilt is not a reliable measure of the size of a sin. David prayed, “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23). He asked God to search him, rather than appointing himself as his own endless investigator.

An example

A married man in his forties commutes by train. Most mornings he sees an attractive woman on the platform. He has never spoken to her, never imagined anything about her, and does not want to. But each time he notices her, he spends the journey feeling sick with guilt. He has started standing at the far end of the platform, and he now dreads the commute. When he finally mentions it to an older friend at church, the friend listens and then asks gently, “What exactly do you think you did wrong?” He opens his mouth, and finds he does not know.

A kinder voice

If this is you, hear this first. Your desire to be pure is a gift of God’s Spirit. But the Lord who gave you that desire is not the voice that follows you around all day with a vague accusation. Jesus describes himself as “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and he promises rest, not a permanent cloud. The rest of this study is an invitation to come out from under it, not by lowering the standard, but by seeing it clearly.

For reflection

What usually happens in you after you notice an attractive person? Can you tell the difference between noticing, being tempted and lusting in your own experience? Where might your sensitivity in this area have come from? What would it mean to let God do the searching, rather than searching yourself all day?

2.title: Beauty Is God’s Idea
2.essay:
Before we speak about lust, we need to speak about beauty. Lust is a twisting of something good, and if we do not know what the good thing is, we will end up suspicious of the good thing itself. Beauty, including the beauty of human faces and bodies, is God’s idea.

Very good

When God finished his work of creation, including the man and the woman made in his image, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). God is not embarrassed by the bodies he made. He shaped them, and he called them good. “He has made everything beautiful in its time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). The beauty of a human person is a small reflection of the beauty of the Maker. David’s great longing was “to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4), and every lesser beauty is a signpost pointing there.

This means that to see beauty and recognise it is not a fall into sin. It is simply to see truly. A person who could look at a lovely face and see nothing would not be holier. He would be seeing less of what God made.

Scripture says so plainly

The Bible is remarkably unembarrassed about human beauty. It tells us that “Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance” (Genesis 29:17). It says that Abigail “was discerning and beautiful” (1 Samuel 25:3), and that Esther “had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at” (Esther 2:7). Nor is it only women. “Joseph was handsome in form and appearance” (Genesis 39:6), and when young David was brought in from the sheep, “he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome” (1 Samuel 16:12).

Think about what this means. The Holy Spirit, who inspired Scripture, noticed that these people were attractive, and wanted us to notice too. The writers were not sinning when they recorded it, and we are not sinning when we read it. Noticing beauty and naming it is something the Bible itself does.

The Song of Songs

One whole book of the Bible is a celebration of love between a man and a woman, physical delight included. “Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:15), says the man, and she answers, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful” (Song of Songs 1:16). This commentary reads the Song first in its plain sense, as a song of married love, while hearing in it the echo of Christ and his church that every marriage carries. Its presence in the Bible tells us that God is not the enemy of attraction. He designed it, and he gave it its proper home.

Good, but not ultimate

Scripture also puts beauty in its place. When Samuel was impressed by the looks of David’s older brother, God told him, “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). Beauty is real but passing. It is not the measure of a person’s worth, and it is not to be grasped or owned. The problem is never that we see beauty, but what we do with it.

The same Bible that notices Rachel’s beauty also shows us David on the roof, seeing a woman who was “very beautiful” (2 Samuel 11:2). Her beauty was not the sin. The sin was in what David did next, as the next chapter will show.

Tempted, yet without sin

There is one more truth we need here, and it is a great comfort. Jesus was fully human. He had eyes, and he lived among men and women, many of them attractive. And the letter to the Hebrews tells us that he “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Every respect. That means that temptation itself, the pull, the invitation, the suggestion, is not sin. If it were, Jesus could not have been tempted and remained sinless. He felt the pressure of temptation without once giving way.

So the Saviour you come to is not a stranger to your struggle. “Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). He does not look at your daily battle with disgust. He looks at it with sympathy, as one who has been there and won.

An example

A woman in her thirties grew up in a church where any comment on someone’s looks was treated as worldly. She now feels a flush of guilt whenever she notices a good-looking man. Reading through Genesis with her small group, she is surprised to find how often Scripture mentions that someone was beautiful or handsome. She says, half laughing, “So the Bible notices too.” It is the beginning of a quieter conscience.

Received with thanksgiving

Paul wrote that “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). His point concerned food and marriage, but the principle reaches wider. The right response to the goodness God has made is not suspicion but thanks. The beauty you notice is God’s handiwork. It is meant to lift your eyes to him.

For reflection

Did you know that Scripture describes so many people as beautiful or handsome? What does that tell you about God’s view of noticing beauty? What does it mean to you that Jesus was tempted in every respect, yet without sin? How could thanksgiving change the way you respond to beauty?

3.title: What Jesus Actually Forbids
3.essay:
Jesus’ words about lustful looking are some of the most searching he ever spoke. They should not be explained away. But neither should they be made to say more than they say. Read carefully, they are both stricter and more freeing than many of us have thought.

Looking with lustful intent

“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Jesus is teaching that the seventh commandment reaches beyond the act to the heart. Adultery begins inside long before it reaches a bedroom.

But notice what he says. Not “everyone who sees a woman”, nor “everyone who notices she is beautiful”, but everyone who looks “with lustful intent”. The Greek phrase means looking in order to desire her, looking with a view to wanting her. The verb Jesus uses for desire is the same one used in the Greek Old Testament for the tenth commandment: “you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:17). To covet is to want to possess what is not yours. Lustful looking is the eye in the service of that coveting. It looks at a person and, in imagination, takes them.

The same is true, of course, when a woman looks at a man in this way. Jesus speaks to the men in front of him, but the principle is for everyone.

The look that dwells

Job made a vow: “I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?” (Job 31:1). The word is gaze. Job did not promise never to see a young woman. He promised not to fix his eyes on her with desire, not to let his look linger and feed.

David on the roof shows how the dwelling look grows. He “saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful” (2 Samuel 11:2). So far, nothing is said against him. But he did not turn away. He kept looking, then “sent and inquired about the woman” (2 Samuel 11:3), and then “sent messengers and took her” (2 Samuel 11:4). The first sight became a stare, the stare became a plan, and the plan became a taking. That is lust: a desire that moves from seeing to possessing.

Desire conceived

James describes the same process: “But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:14–15). There is a difference between being lured and conceiving. The lure is the temptation, which comes to us. Conception is the moment we welcome it, agree with it and let it grow. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation traces these steps more fully.

A saying often attributed to Martin Luther puts it memorably. You cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. The first passing thought, the first noticing, even the first flicker of temptation, are birds flying over. Lust is the nest: the thought invited to stay, furnished and lived in.

Tear it out

Jesus goes on: “If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29). This is deliberate overstatement, a vivid way of saying, “Deal ruthlessly with whatever leads you into sin.” He is not commanding self-harm, but he is serious. If certain websites, films, habits or friendships regularly lead you into lust, cut them off.

Notice, though, what this command is aimed at: whatever “causes you to sin”. It is not aimed at the ordinary sight of men and women as you go about your day. A sensitive conscience can easily turn Jesus’ call into a campaign against normal living, and that is not what he meant.

A disputed question

Christians have long asked whether the very first stirrings of wrong desire, which arise before we have chosen anything, are themselves sin. Roman Catholic teaching holds that the inclination to sin left in the baptised, which it calls concupiscence, is not properly sin until the will consents. The Reformers and the Westminster Confession taught that the corruption of our nature remaining in believers, and its first motions, are truly sin, though pardoned in Christ. Others, especially in some holiness traditions, have held that the believer can be largely freed from such stirrings in this life.

This commentary’s view: Noticing beauty is not sin at all. Being tempted is not sin, as Hebrews 4:15 shows. The fallen nature from which wrong desires arise is sin, which every believer fights and grieves over, but it is wholly covered by Christ and brings no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Consenting to temptation, choosing to look in order to desire and to dwell in fantasy, is the sin Jesus names, and it calls for repentance. The fact that we still have a fallen nature is a reason to cling to Christ, not a reason to treat every glance as a fresh offence.

An example

A young married man asks his pastor whether he has “committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28) because he noticed that a woman at the gym was attractive. The pastor asks him three questions. Did you keep looking in order to want her? Did you imagine anything? Did you go back for another look? The answer to each is no. “Then you saw her,” the pastor says. “You did not lust after her. And the fact that you are this troubled shows how much you love your wife.”

For reflection

How does the phrase “with lustful intent” change the way you read Matthew 5:28? What is the difference between seeing, as David first did, and what David did next? In your own life, where are the birds flying over, and where, if anywhere, are they building a nest? What, if anything, does Jesus’ call to “tear it out” require of you?

4.title: False Guilt and True Guilt
4.essay:
God gave us a conscience to warn us when we do wrong. It is a precious gift. But like a smoke alarm that goes off whenever you make toast, a conscience can be set wrongly, sounding the alarm where there is no fire. Learning to tell the difference between true guilt and false guilt is part of growing up in Christ.

The conscience can be wrong

Paul knew that conscience can be miscalibrated. In Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 he speaks of believers with a “weak” conscience, who thought eating certain food would defile them. Some, he says, “through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled” (1 Corinthians 8:7). Their consciences condemned what God did not condemn. Paul says, “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean” (Romans 14:14).

Paul told the strong to be patient with such believers, but he also showed that a weak conscience needs to be taught by God’s word, so that it accuses only where God accuses. A conscience that condemns every glance is like those believers who would not eat meat: sincere, but mistaken about what God requires.

Even a clear conscience is not the final judge. Paul wrote, “For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4). The same is true the other way round. A heavy conscience does not prove you guilty. The Lord is the judge, and his word is the standard.

God is greater than our heart

John wrote to Christians whose hearts were troubled. “By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:19–20). This is a remarkable promise. Your heart may condemn you, but your heart is not God. He is greater, and he knows everything: he knows what really happened in that moment on the street, he knows your desire to please him, and he knows that the blood of his Son has covered all your sin. When your heart and God disagree, God wins.

Two voices

True guilt and false guilt feel different when you learn to listen. The Holy Spirit’s conviction is specific: it names a real sin, such as “You kept looking at her in order to want her.” It leads you to confess, and then it lifts, because Christ has dealt with that sin. False guilt is vague: “You are dirty. You are a bad husband. Something is wrong with you.” It never names anything you can confess, and it never lifts, however much you pray.

Scripture calls Satan “the accuser of our brothers … who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10). Not every vague cloud of guilt comes from him. Some comes from our temperament or upbringing. But he is glad to use it. If he cannot draw you into lust, he will try to make you miserable about lust you have not committed. The study The Truth About Sin has a fuller section on telling conviction from condemnation, and the study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation deals with the habit of not forgiving yourself.

When the alarm will not stop

For some people this goes further. The thought, “Did I lust? Was that sinful?” becomes sticky and constant. They check their feelings again and again. They confess the same glance many times. They ask a spouse or friend for reassurance, feel better for an hour, then need to ask again. Sometimes unwanted sexual thoughts or images flash into the mind, thoughts they find horrible, and the very horror makes them return more often.

This pattern has a name. Christians have long called it scrupulosity, a tormented over-sensitivity of conscience. Today it is often recognised as a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and unwanted sexual thoughts are one of its most common themes. The key point is this: intrusive thoughts that you hate and do not want are not lust. Lust welcomes the thought. The person with intrusive thoughts is fighting it with all their strength.

If this describes you, please speak to your doctor or a qualified counsellor, ideally one who understands both OCD and Christian faith. This is common and very treatable. There are well-tested therapies, and sometimes medicine helps. Seeking such help is no failure of faith. God often gives healing through such means, and a wise pastor will be glad to walk with you alongside them. If your distress ever turns to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now: call the emergency services or a crisis line, and tell someone you trust.

An example

A married woman found that after noticing any good-looking man, she would spend hours asking herself whether she had felt attraction, and would confess to God again and again. Her pastor recognised the pattern and encouraged her to see her doctor, who referred her to a counsellor experienced in OCD. Over some months she learned to let the questions go unanswered rather than checking. The thoughts became quieter. She told her pastor that she had come to see her relentless checking as fear rather than holiness.

True guilt is good news too

None of this means real lust does not happen. It does, and when it does, true guilt is a mercy, because it leads us to a Saviour who forgives. The aim is not a conscience that never speaks, but one that speaks truly: one that is quiet when we have done nothing wrong, and clear when we have, so that we can confess, be forgiven and move on.

For reflection

Is your conscience more like a well-set alarm or one that goes off at toast? How does 1 John 3:19–20 speak to a heart that condemns you? Can you tell the difference between specific conviction and vague accusation in your own experience? Do you recognise any of the signs of scrupulosity, and if so, who could you talk to?

5.title: A Clean Conscience in Christ
5.essay:
The deepest answer to a troubled conscience is not a better technique for managing guilt. It is a person. Jesus Christ lived the pure life we have not lived, died for the impure thoughts and looks we have indulged, and now stands before the Father for us. In him, the conscience can be truly clean.

No condemnation

Paul’s great declaration is for you: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Not condemnation for most sins, or for sins you have managed to confess properly. None. The reason is not that you have kept your eyes perfectly, but that Christ has. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Every lustful look you have ever given, and every one you will give, was laid on him. His perfect purity is counted as yours.

Jesus’ eyes never once looked at a woman to possess her. He was “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). And that spotless purity is now the clothing God sees on you. “Remove the filthy garments from him,” said the angel to the high priest Joshua, and then, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). That is what God has done for every believer.

A cleansed conscience

The letter to the Hebrews speaks directly to the conscience. Old covenant sacrifices could cleanse the body, but not the conscience. Christ’s sacrifice reaches deeper: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). And so we are invited to “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience” (Hebrews 10:22).

A clean conscience is not one that feels nothing. It is one that has been washed by Christ and believes it. When the cloud descends, you do not have to work your way out of it by examining yourself for hours. You can look away from yourself to the blood that has already been shed, and to the Saviour who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25) for you. “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died … who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

How Jesus looked at women

The Gospels give us glimpses of how the pure Son of God looked at women. He was not afraid of them. He spoke with a Samaritan woman alone at a well, and his disciples “marveled that he was talking with a woman” (John 4:27). When a woman with a sinful reputation wept at his feet, the religious host saw only a scandal. Jesus turned to her and said to him, “Do you see this woman?” (Luke 7:44). Simon saw a category and a threat. Jesus saw a person, a forgiven daughter.

His purity did not make him distant or cold. It made him free: free to look at women with honour, to speak with them, to welcome them among his followers, and to love them truly. That is the purity he is working in us. Not a nervous avoidance, but a clean and generous gaze.

Sisters and mothers

Paul told Timothy to treat “older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). That little phrase is a whole way of seeing. In Christ, the women around a believing man are not objects to be consumed and not threats to be feared. They are family. You notice your sister is beautiful, and you are glad for her. You do not want to take anything from her. You want her good. The same is true for a woman looking at the men in her church family as fathers and brothers.

Underneath this is a deeper truth. Every person you see is made in God’s image. “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Lust reduces an image-bearer to a body. Fear reduces an image-bearer to a danger. The gospel restores them to what they are: people loved by God, for whom you can pray, whom you can serve and honour.

An example

A man who had struggled with guilt after every glance began to pray a simple prayer whenever he noticed an attractive woman: “Lord, bless her. Be good to her today.” He found that it changed the way he saw people. Instead of a moment of danger, it became a moment of goodwill. The woman on the bus became a person with troubles and hopes of her own, and he could wish her well and move on.

Beholding him

In the end, the cure for lust and for false guilt is the same: to see Christ. “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Lust is a hunger looking for its food in the wrong place. Guilt is a fear that has not yet seen how complete forgiveness is. Both are answered by the beauty of the one who is altogether lovely, who gave himself for us, and who will one day present us to himself spotless. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). That purity is his gift, and that sight is our future.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Christ’s purity is counted as yours? How does Hebrews 9:14 speak to your conscience? What strikes you about the way Jesus looked at and spoke with women? How might praying for the people you notice change the way you see them?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
The truths of the gospel are meant for the street, the office and the train platform, not only for quiet times. Here is some practical wisdom for the moment you notice someone, for the times you do fall into lust, and for the long hours when the cloud lingers. These are not new rules to perform, but ways of living out the freedom Christ has given.

In the moment

Notice, and let it be. You have seen that someone is attractive. That is all that has happened. You do not need to panic or repent. Give thanks, or simply move on. Sometimes a brief “Thank you, Lord, for the beauty you have made” is a good response. Sometimes it is better simply to carry on with what you were doing. Either is fine.

Turn your gaze. If you feel a pull to keep looking, look elsewhere. “Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways” (Psalm 119:37). Not a frantic jerk of the head, just a calm turning to the next thing. Pray briefly, if you feel tempted: “Lord, keep my heart. Bless her.” Refuse the second look and the fantasy. This is where the real battle is. The first look is not the problem; the deliberate second look, or the story your imagination wants to tell, is where you say no.

Do not interrogate yourself. This matters as much as anything here. Once you have turned away, do not go back over the moment asking whether you looked too long or felt too much. That replay keeps the person in your mind far longer than the glance ever did, and it feeds the cloud. Leave it with God and get on with your day.

When you do fall

Sometimes you will lust. You will take the second look, or let the fantasy run. When that happens, be honest and quick. Confess it plainly to God: not a vague “I’m so bad,” but “Lord, I looked to desire, and I let my mind dwell on her. I am sorry.” Then believe the promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). David prayed, “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). The forgiveness is immediate.

Then get up and do not wallow. Godly grief leads to repentance; worldly grief “produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Wallowing is not deeper repentance. “If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Let him have the last word, and turn to the next good thing. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation has a chapter on what to do when you fall.

Delight in your spouse

For married believers, the best protection against wandering desire is not only saying no to others, but saying yes to your husband or wife. “Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love” (Proverbs 5:18–19). Scripture commands delight. “Enjoy life with the wife whom you love” (Ecclesiastes 9:9).

Cultivate that delight. Tell your spouse what you find beautiful in them. Notice them as carefully as you notice anything else. Pursue them, spend time together, give yourselves to one another physically as Paul urges (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). A growing love at home makes the noticing elsewhere smaller and quieter. The study Christian Marriage says much more. For single believers, delight in God’s good gifts and in the family of the church, and the study Biblical Sexuality has a chapter on singleness.

Wise boundaries without fear

Some boundaries are simply wise. If pornography or certain kinds of media have been a struggle, use filters and accountability software, keep devices out of the bedroom, and tell a trusted friend who will ask you how you are doing. If a particular friendship is becoming emotionally intimate in ways that belong to marriage, step back. These are the real cuttings-off that Jesus calls for.

But do not let boundaries become fear-driven avoidance. Refusing to look women in the eye, being cold to female colleagues, or avoiding half the church is not holiness. Paul warned against rules that have “an appearance of wisdom” but “are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). Treating every woman as a danger is not how Jesus lived, and it is unkind to the women themselves. Aim for the warm, honourable freedom of brothers and sisters.

Quieting the cloud

When the cloud lingers after a glance, ask yourself one question: did I choose to look in order to desire, or dwell in fantasy? If yes, confess it and receive forgiveness. If no, there is nothing to confess. Tell yourself so, and then turn your mind elsewhere. “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, … think about these things” (Philippians 4:8).

You might keep a verse ready: “There is therefore now no condemnation” (Romans 8:1), or “God is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20). Pray, “Lord, if I sinned, forgive me. If I did not, take this feeling away. Either way, I am yours.” Then let it go, even if the feeling has not gone. Feelings often lag behind faith. And if the cloud keeps coming back daily despite all this, please talk to a pastor and a doctor or counsellor, as the fourth chapter suggests.

An example

The commuter from the first chapter began to try some of this. When he saw the woman on the platform, he would pray, “Lord, bless her today,” and then turn to his book. When the old guilt rose, he would ask, “Did I choose to look to desire?” and answer honestly, “No.” He told his wife, and she was relieved rather than hurt. Some mornings the cloud still came, but it lifted much sooner. One day he noticed he had forgotten all about it until the train pulled into the city.

Growth here takes time, and the old reflex will return now and then. That is not defeat. Each time you notice beauty without fear, refuse the second look without panic, or confess real sin and believe you are forgiven, you are learning to live as what you already are in Christ: clean, loved and free.

For reflection

Which of the steps for the moment do you most need to practise? What would it look like for you to stop interrogating yourself after a glance? If you are married, how could you grow in delight in your spouse this week? Are there boundaries you need, or fear-driven avoidances you need to let go?
